item.title: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines: a guide to semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide
item.description: Key takeaways: semaglutide and tirzepatide are approved medicines; retatrutide is still in trials and approved nowhere. item.title: KLOW 80: what is in the vial and what we don't know
item.description: KLOW is a blend of four peptides in one vial: GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. The 80 is the total mass in milligrams. item.title: The July 2026 FDA committee vote: what it really means for BPC-157 and others
item.description: On 22–23 July 2026 the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) reviewed seven peptides. It backed six: BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV (each 8 to 6 with one abstention), plus MOTS-c, Semax and Epitalon. It rejected DSIP (emideltide) 6 to 7.

item.title: Amino acid, peptide, protein: what is the difference
item.description: Amino acids are the building blocks. Humans use 20 standard amino acids, each with an amino and a carboxyl group. When the carboxyl group of one joins the amino group of the next, a peptide bond forms and a molecule of water is released.

item.title: Peptides in cosmetics: studies versus marketing
item.description: Manufacturers usually split cosmetic peptides into signal peptides (meant to prompt skin cells to make collagen), carrier peptides such as copper-binding GHK-Cu, and neuromodulating ones such as acetyl hexapeptide-8, marketed as “Botox in a cream”.

item.title: Collagen powder: what the studies show
item.description: Hydrolyzed collagen is collagen broken by enzymes into short peptides. In the gut it is digested further into amino acids and di- and tripeptides, and some short fragments have been detected in blood after eating.

item.title: “Research use only” peptides: why they are a bad idea
item.description: Peptides labelled “for laboratory research only”, such as BPC-157, are sold online. Many are not approved as drugs. Such products need not meet drug manufacturing standards, so contents, purity, strength and sterility are hard to verify.
